method: Each claim checked against the retrieved text of the ACSQHC Stroke Clinical Care Standard (updated 11 June 2026), including the eight quality statements, the for-clinicians/for-services/for-consumers sections, the full indicator list, the updates section and the scope section. The Standard defers all thrombolysis and thrombectomy time windows, ICH blood pressure targets and reversal agents to the Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management; none were retrieved and none are reconstructed here. The National Acute Stroke Services Framework, which defines a capable hospital and a stroke unit, was not retrieved. Therapeutic Guidelines' stroke topic is cited by the Standard and is licensed content, cited by reference only and not reproduced. Retrieved text contains extraction artefacts where double-n collapsed ('pla ing' for planning, 'scree ' for screen, 'occlusio ' for occlusion); source_text is preserved verbatim and the guideline renders the evident word.

claims.claim: The Stroke Clinical Care Standard was updated in June 2026, was first released in 2015 with a minor update in 2019, and the revised Standard incorporates changes in the relevant evidence-based guidelines since 2019
claims.source_text: The Stroke Clinical Care Standard was updated in June 2026. It was first released in 2015 with a minor update in 2019. This revised Clinical Care Standard incorporates changes in the relevant evidence-based guidelines since 2019.

claims.claim: Key updates in the current version include a change of title, previously the Acute Stroke Clinical Care Standard, to include aspects of care extending beyond the acute and hyperacute phase, addition of cultural safety and equity considerations, broader inclusion of stroke telehealth in hyperacute and acute stroke care, greater emphasis on ambulance services and pre-hospital notification systems, inclusion of time-critical care for intracerebral haemorrhage, greater emphasis on rehabilitation, amendments to improve timely access to stroke unit care and early protocolised care, and a new quality statement about follow-up
claims.source_text: change of title, previously the 'Acute Stroke Clinical Care Standard', to include aspects of care extending beyond the acute and hyperacute phasen- addition of cultural safety and equity considerationsn- broader inclusion of stroke telehealth in hyperacute and acute stroke caren- greater emphasis on ambulance services and pre-hospital notification systemsn- inclusion of time-critical care for intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)n- greater emphasis on rehabilitation, including assessment of needs, initiation in hospital and pla ing arrangements for ongoing care post dischargen- amendments to improve timely access to stroke unit care and early, protocolised caren- a new quality statement about follow-up.

claims.claim: Key updates to the indicators include the addition of indicators to measure provision of time-critical care, delivery of stroke unit care, multidisciplinary assessment to identify rehabilitation needs, referral for ongoing rehabilitation and participation in a follow-up review, the retiring of four indicators, and revisions to several indicators
claims.source_text: the addition of indicators to measure:n- provision of time-critical caren- delivery of stroke unit caren- multidisciplinary assessment to identify rehabilitation needsn- referral for ongoing rehabilitatio - participation in a follow-up reviewn- the retiring of four indicatorsn- revisions to several indicators.

claims.claim: The Standard does not cover transient ischaemic attack, subarachnoid, extradural or subdural haemorrhage, intracerebral haemorrhage secondary to a structural abnormality in the brain, or the care of children with stroke
claims.source_text: This Standard does not cover: - transient ischaemic attack (TIA)n- subarachnoid, extradural or subdural haemorrhagen- intracerebral haemorrhage secondary to a structural abnormality in the brain (such as an arteriovenous malformation, intracranial aneurysm, tumour, trauma, or previous cerebral infarction)n- the care of children with stroke.

claims.claim: The Standard does not offer specific guidance on end-of-life or palliative care for patients who have had a stroke and refers to the National Consensus Statement on essential elements for safe and high-quality end-of-life care
claims.source_text: This Standard does not offer specific guidance on end-of-life or palliative care for patients who have had a stroke. See the National Consensus Statement: Essential elements for safe and high‑quality end‑of‑life care.

claims.claim: Quality statement 1 states that a person with suspected stroke is assessed using a validated stroke screening tool such as the F.A.S.T. test, that when acute stroke is suspected the person is transported immediately to a hospital capable of providing appropriate time-critical therapy, and that the hospital is pre-notified to enable rapid access to care
claims.source_text: ted stroke screening tool, such as the F.A.S.T. (Face, Arms, Speech and Time) test. When acute stroke is suspected, the person is transported immediately to a hospital capable of providing appropriate time-critical therapy. The hospital is pre-notified to enable rapid access to care.

claims.claim: The Standard notes that F.A.S.T. is a useful tool for identifying stroke particularly for non-clinicians, however other tools may have greater accuracy in detecting acute ischaemic stroke
claims.source_text: Note that F.A.S.T. is a useful tool for identifying stroke, particularly for non-clinicians. However, other tools may have greater accuracy in detecting acute ischaemic stroke (see Related Resources).

claims.claim: Validated stroke screening tools named by the Standard include BE-FAST, CRESST, F.A.S.T., MASS and ROSIER, and other validated tools used in the assessment of stroke include ACT-FAST for identification of large vessel occlusion, HUNTER-8 or NIHSS-8 for quantifying impairment, the modified Rankin Scale for measuring premorbid function, and RACE for large vessel occlusion identification
claims.source_text: Validated stroke screening tools include (in alphabetical order): - BE-FAST – Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Timen- CRESST – Canberra pREhospital Stroke Screening Tooln- F.A.S.T. – Face, Arms, Speech, Timen- MASS – Melbourne Ambulance Stroke Scree - ROSIER – Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room Other validated tools used in the assessment of stroke include (in alphabetical order): - ACT-FAST – for identification of large vessel occlusio - HUNTER-8 or NIHSS-8 – for quantifying the impairment caused by stroken- Modified Rankin Scale or mRS – for measuring premorbid functio - RACE – Rapid Arterial Occlusion Evaluation (large vessel occlusion identification tool)

claims.claim: Once a patient is suspected of having an acute stroke, meaning clinical signs less than 24 hours, clinicians should expedite primary emergency transport usually by ambulance to a hospital capable of providing time-critical stroke therapy
claims.source_text: Once a patient is suspected of having an acute (clinical signs less than 24 hours) stroke, expedite primary emergency transport (usually by ambulance) to a hospital capable of providing time-critical stroke therapy.

claims.claim: Pre-hospital clinicians including ambulance services should use pre-notification systems and bypass to access hospitals capable of providing appropriate time-critical stroke therapies including thrombolysis when required
claims.source_text: Pre-hospital clinicians**, including ambulance services, should use pre-notification systems and bypass to access hospitals capable of providing appropriate time-critical stroke therapies (including thrombolysis) when required.

claims.claim: Ambulances should have agreed bypass protocols to transport people to a Comprehensive Stroke Centre in the case of patients with suspected large vessel occlusion
claims.source_text: Ambulances should have agreed bypass protocols to transport people to a Comprehensive Stroke Centre (CSC) in the case of patients with suspected large vessel occlusion.

claims.claim: Pre-hospital clinicians should follow local recommended protocols which may include documenting symptom discovery, last known well time, time of ambulance arrival on scene and medication history
claims.source_text: Follow local recommended protocols to help prepare the patient for rapid treatment, which may include documenting symptom discovery, last known 'well' time, time of ambulance arrival on scene and medication history

claims.claim: Hospital-based teams should prepare for patient arrival when pre-notified by obtaining medical records and a best possible medication history, contacting next of kin for more details, activating a Code Stroke alert system, and facilitating access to CT imaging for urgent assessment
claims.source_text: Hospital-based teams** should prepare for patient arrival when pre-notified, by obtaining medical records and a best possible medication history, contacting next of kin for more details, activating a 'Code Stroke' alert system, and facilitating access to CT imaging for urgent assessment.

claims.claim: More detailed stroke severity scales such as the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale may be used in hospital but are not recommended in the pre-hospital setting
claims.source_text: More detailed stroke severity scales (for example, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS]) may be used in hospital but are not recommended in the pre-hospital setting.

claims.claim: Exceptions to urgent transport include patients for whom transfer would not be consistent with their goals of care or advanced care plan, such as palliative care patients
claims.source_text: Exceptions include patients for whom transfer would not be consistent with their goals of care or advanced care plan, such as palliative care patients.

claims.claim: Quality statement 2 states that a patient with acute stroke receives time-critical therapy urgently and in accordance with the Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management, that a patient with ischaemic stroke suitable for reperfusion therapy receives timely thrombolysis and/or endovascular thrombectomy, and that a patient with intracerebral haemorrhage receives urgent blood-pressure-lowering therapy and/or anticoagulation reversal where appropriate
claims.source_text: A patient with acute stroke receives time-critical therapy urgently and in accordance with the Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management. A patient with ischaemic stroke suitable for reperfusion therapy receives timely thrombolysis and/or endovascular thrombectomy. A patient with intracerebral haemorrhage receives urgent blood-pressure-lowering therapy and/or anticoagulation reversal where appropriate.

claims.claim: Clinicians should consider reperfusion treatment for all patients with ischaemic stroke and, as clinically indicated, offer thrombolysis and/or endovascular thrombectomy within the time frames recommended in the current Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
claims.source_text: Consider reperfusion treatment for all patients with ischaemic stroke. As clinically indicated, offer thrombolysis and/or endovascular thrombectomy within the time frames recommended in the current Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management.

claims.claim: To enable appropriate reperfusion clinicians should use multimodal imaging, being non-contrast CT and both CT angiogram and CT perfusion, when possible to identify candidates for endovascular thrombectomy or surgical treatments
claims.source_text: To enable appropriate reperfusion, use multimodal imaging (Non-Contrast CT [NCCT], and both CT angiogram and CT perfusion) when possible to identify candidates for endovascular thrombectomy or surgical treatments.

claims.claim: As part of transfer for endovascular thrombectomy clinicians should ensure all imaging including any CT angiogram is transferred to the treating hospital rapidly to facilitate treatment on arrival
claims.source_text: ensure all imaging (including any CT angiogram) is transferred to the treating hospital rapidly to facilitate treatment on arrival.

claims.claim: In hospitals that do not provide 24-hour on-site access to stroke specialists, telestroke systems should be used to assist with patient assessment and decision-making regarding acute thrombolytic therapy and possible transfer for endovascular thrombectomy
claims.source_text: In hospitals that do not provide 24-hour, on-site access to stroke specialists, use telestroke systems to assist with patient assessment and decision-making regarding acute thrombolytic therapy and possible transfer for endovascular thrombectomy.

claims.claim: If an intracerebral haemorrhage is identified after imaging and if clinically indicated, clinicians should promptly initiate control of blood pressure and reversal of coagulopathy within the targets and timeframes recommended in the current Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
claims.source_text: If an intracerebral haemorrhage is identified after imaging, and if clinically indicated, promptly initiate control of blood pressure and reversal of coagulopathy within the targets and timeframes recommended in the current Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management.

claims.claim: Clinicians should arrange urgent vascular imaging such as CT angiography, magnetic resonance angiography or digital subtraction angiography to identify patients who may need specific specialist treatment such as management of bleeds secondary to vascular malformations, and refer for neurosurgical consultation using the local stroke network and referral pathway
claims.source_text: Arrange urgent vascular imaging (such as CT angiography, magnetic resonance angiography or digital subtraction angiography) to identify patients who may need specific specialist treatment, such as management of bleeds secondary to vascular malformations. Refer for neurosurgical consultation using your local stroke network and referral pathway.

claims.claim: If time-critical therapy is not provided, the reason should be documented in the patient's medical record
claims.source_text: If time-critical therapy is not provided, document the reason in the patient's medical record.

claims.claim: Quality statement 3 states that a patient with stroke is promptly transferred to a stroke unit as defined in the National Acute Stroke Services Framework and receives early protocolised care to prevent complications and maximise recovery
claims.source_text: A patient with stroke is promptly transferred to a stroke unit, as defined in the National Acute Stroke Services Framework. The patient receives early, protocolised care to prevent complications and maximise recovery.

claims.claim: Stroke unit care is organised care within a specific ward in a hospital provided by a multidisciplinary team who specialise in stroke management, and care quality is recorded and guided by established protocols
claims.source_text: Stroke unit care is organised care within a specific ward in a hospital. It is provided by a multidisciplinary team who specialise in stroke management, coordinating diagnostic work-up and treatment, early mobilisation and rehabilitation and secondary prevention. This team works with the patient and family during the inpatient stay. Care quality is recorded and guided by established protocols.

claims.claim: People with stroke who receive care in a dedicated stroke unit are more likely to be alive, living at home, and independently looking after themselves one year after their stroke
claims.source_text: People with stroke who receive care in a dedicated stroke unit are more likely to be alive, living at home, and independently looking after themselves one year after their stroke.

claims.claim: Intensive care units, high dependency units or similar locations are appropriate alternatives to stroke unit care for patients requiring critical care management
claims.source_text: Intensive care units (ICUs), high dependency units (HDUs) or similar locations are appropriate alternatives to stroke unit care for patients requiring critical care management.

claims.claim: If there is no stroke unit at the healthcare service, patients should receive guideline-recommended care and protocols in the nearest similar unit able to meet the requirements for stroke unit care, which may include management on the ward where the patient is located with access to a telestroke service and allied health assessment
claims.source_text: If there is no stroke unit at the healthcare service, patients should receive guideline-recommended care and protocols in the nearest similar unit able to meet the requirements for stroke unit care. This may include management on the ward where the patient is located, with access to a telestroke service and allied health assessment.

claims.claim: Early protocolised stroke care should include screening for swallowing difficulties within four hours of arrival to hospital using a validated screening tool before giving patients food, fluids or oral medications, monitoring and prompt management of pyrexia and hyperglycaemia for the first 72 hours, screening for communication difficulties, and ensuring appropriate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis
claims.source_text: screening for swallowing difficulties within four hours of arrival to hospital using a validated screening tool before giving patients food, fluids or oral medicationsn- monitoring and prompt management of pyrexia and hyperglycaemia for the first 72 hoursn- screening for communication difficultiesn- ensuring appropriate venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis

claims.claim: Escalation pathways should include review by a speech pathologist if swallowing or communication difficulties are identified and notifying medical officers if the patient has body temperature or glucose levels outside the recommended parameters
claims.source_text: following escalation pathways within the above protocols (such as review by a speech pathologist if swallowing or communication difficulties are identified), and notifying medical officers if the patient has body temperature or glucose levels outside the recommended parameters

claims.claim: The Standard names the FeSS fever, sugar and swallowing clinical treatment protocols as a bundle of care for monitoring and managing pyrexia, hyperglycaemia and swallowing difficulties, and names the Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard for VTE prophylaxis
claims.source_text: FeSS (Fever, Sugar and Swallowing) clinical treatment protocols and implementation strategy (bundle of care for monitoring and managing pyrexia, hyperglycaemia and swallowing difficulties)n- Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard (for VTE prophylaxis)

claims.claim: All clinicians should use supportive communication techniques with patients who have communication difficulties, which improves patient consent processes, patients' ability to express their needs and preferences, and patient engagement with care
claims.source_text: All clinicians should use supportive communication techniques with patients who have communication difficulties. This improves patient consent processes, patients' ability to express their needs and preferences, and patient engagement with care.

claims.claim: Quality statement 4 states that a patient's initial rehabilitation needs are assessed by a multidisciplinary team as early as possible and within 48 hours of hospital admission for stroke, that individualised guideline-recommended rehabilitation begins as soon as clinically appropriate during the admission, that rehabilitation needs are continually assessed and documented, and that arrangements for ongoing rehabilitation are made before discharge
claims.source_text: A patient's initial rehabilitation needs are assessed by a multidisciplinary team as early as possible and within 48 hours of hospital admission for stroke. Individualised, guideline-recommended rehabilitation begins as soon as clinically appropriate during the admission. Rehabilitation needs are continually assessed and documented. Arrangements for ongoing rehabilitation are made before discharge.

claims.claim: Intensive early mobilisation within 24 hours of stroke onset is not recommended
claims.source_text: **Note**: Intensive early mobilisation within 24 hours of stroke onset is not recommended.

claims.claim: The rehabilitation assessment should include but not be limited to medical including rehabilitation medicine, nursing, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, speech pathology, dietetics, and clinical psychology
claims.source_text: These should include, but not be limited to, medical (including rehabilitation medicine), nursing, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, speech pathology, dietetics, and clinical psychology.

claims.claim: While the patient is in hospital functional status should be recorded using a validated tool such as the Functional Independence Measure, modified Rankin Scale, Barthel Index, or Functional Autonomy Measurement System
claims.source_text: While the patient is in hospital, record functional status using a validated tool such as the Functional Independence Measure (FIM), modified Rankin Scale (mRS), Barthel Index, or Functional Autonomy Measurement System (SMAF).

claims.claim: Throughout the hospital admission the multidisciplinary team should continually re-assess the patient's rehabilitation needs especially before discharge, considering changes in the patient's mood and cognition such as difficulty with concentration, memory loss, and language issues
claims.source_text: Throughout the hospital admission, the multidisciplinary team should continually re-assess the patient's rehabilitation needs, especially before discharge. Consider changes in the patient's mood and cognition such as difficulty with concentration, memory loss, and language issues.

claims.claim: Alternative arrangements may apply if the patient is unable or unwilling to participate in rehabilitation, or rehabilitation is not consistent with their goals of care
claims.source_text: Alternative arrangements may apply if the patient is unable or unwilling to participate in rehabilitation, or rehabilitation is not consistent with their goals of care.

claims.claim: Quality statement 5 states that while in hospital a patient undergoes a comprehensive assessment to determine the probable cause of their stroke, and that this assessment informs their ongoing care including individualised treatment and education to promote healthy living and reduce their risk of another stroke
claims.source_text: While in hospital, a patient undergoes a comprehensive assessment to determine the probable cause of their stroke. This assessment informs their ongoing care, including individualised treatment and education to promote healthy living and reduce their risk of another stroke.

claims.claim: Clinicians should communicate with the patient's general practice team to gather information about previous treatments and investigations undertaken, for example their previous response to relevant medicines and results of cardiac monitoring
claims.source_text: Communicate with the patient's general practice team to gather information about previous treatments and investigations undertaken, which may inform their ongoing treatment. For example, their previous response to relevant medicines and results of cardiac monitoring.

claims.claim: Clinicians should offer testing and assessment to investigate the mechanism of the patient's stroke to enable targeted therapies that can minimise the risk of recurrence, for example cardiac assessment and monitoring to screen for atrial fibrillation, and when assessment is not appropriate during the acute admission should refer or arrange for the assessments to be completed promptly after hospital discharge
claims.source_text: Offer testing and assessment to investigate the mechanism of the patient's stroke to enable targeted therapies that can minimise the risk of recurrence (for example, cardiac assessment and monitoring to screen for atrial fibrillation). When assessment is not appropriate during the acute admission, refer or arrange for the assessments to be completed promptly after hospital discharge.

claims.claim: Clinicians should prescribe appropriate medicines for secondary prevention including anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation and antiplatelet, antihypertensive and lipid-lowering medicines where indicated and in line with current guidelines, and other measures may include time-limited surgical interventions such as carotid endarterectomy or closure of a patent foramen ovale in younger patients
claims.source_text: Prescribe appropriate medicines for secondary prevention, including anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation and antiplatelet, antihypertensive and lipid-lowering medicines, where indicated and in line with current guidelines. Other measures may include time-limited surgical interventions (for example, carotid endarterectomy) or closure of a patent foramen ovale in younger patients.

claims.claim: Clinicians should discuss risk factors such as uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes, smoking, poor diet, insufficient physical activity and excessive alcohol or recreational drug use, and provide written information
claims.source_text: Discuss risk factors such as uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes, smoking, poor diet, insufficient physical activity and excessive alcohol or recreational drug use, and provide written information.

claims.claim: Quality statement 6 states that the family and support people of a patient with stroke are provided with information and practical assistance so that they can safely and confidently support the patient to manage their daily needs
claims.source_text: The family and support people of a patient with stroke are provided with information and practical assistance so that they can safely and confidently support the patient to manage their daily needs.

claims.claim: Practical assistance includes advice, guidance and training for families and support people on how to safely support the patient with their new daily needs
claims.source_text: Practical assistance includes advice, guidance and training for families and support people on how to safely support the patient with their new daily needs.

claims.claim: Documenting all care given in the 24-hour period before discharge can help in identifying the patient's support needs when they are discharged to a private residence or a residential aged care facility
claims.source_text: Documenting all care given in the 24-hour period before discharge can help in identifying the patient's support needs when they are discharged to a private residence or a residential aged care facility.

claims.claim: The areas in which a patient may need support include physical care covering personal care techniques, the use of new assistive equipment, modification of food and drink to ensure safe swallowing, and safe mobilisation and transfer; communication and cognition covering communication partner training and strategies to manage changes in memory, concentration and behaviour; psychosocial wellbeing covering fatigue management, emotional support, carer self-care and strategies to return to community life; and system navigation covering support to access respite, carer financial aid, NDIS or My Aged Care, guidance on health and financial decision-making responsibilities, and contact details of support services
claims.source_text: : Personal care techniques, the use of new assistive equipment, modification of food and drink to ensure safe swallowing, and safe mobilisation and transfer.n- Communication and cognition: Communication partner training, and strategies to manage changes in memory, concentration, and behaviour.n- Psychosocial wellbeing: Fatigue management, emotional support, carer self-care, and strategies for both the patient and carer to return to community life.n- System navigation: Support to access respite, carer financial aid, NDIS or My Aged Care, guidance on health and financial decision-making responsibilities, and the contact details of support services.

claims.claim: If a patient is assessed as able to manage independently but does not have an identified carer or support person, clinicians should offer the patient information, support and advice in a way they can understand to help them safely and confidently manage their daily needs
claims.source_text: If a patient is assessed as able to manage independently but does not have an identified carer or support person, offer the patient information, support and advice (in a way they can understand) to help them safely and confidently manage their daily needs.

claims.claim: Quality statement 7 states that before leaving hospital a patient with stroke and their family or support people are involved in the development of an individualised care plan that describes the ongoing care required, and that this care plan is given to the patient, their general practice and their ongoing rehabilitation team at the time of discharge
claims.source_text: Before leaving hospital, a patient with stroke and their family or support people are involved in the development of an individualised care plan that describes the ongoing care required. This care plan is given to the patient, their general practice and their ongoing rehabilitation team at the time of discharge.

claims.claim: The individualised care plan should include results from relevant rehabilitation assessments, ongoing rehabilitation needs and goals and a plan to achieve these, secondary prevention recommendations discussed such as medicines and lifestyle modifications and where possible a medication list and education provided by a pharmacist, information discussed and practical assistance for managing daily activities including advice on when the person may resume driving a vehicle and contact details for support services, and details of referrals and follow-up appointments
claims.source_text: results from relevant rehabilitation assessments, ongoing rehabilitation needs and goals, and a plan to achieve these (see Quality statement 4)n- secondary prevention recommendations discussed, such as medicines and lifestyle modifications (see Quality statement 5), and, where possible, a medication list and education provided by a pharmacistn- information discussed and practical assistance for managing daily activities, advice on when the person may resume driving a vehicle, and contact details for support services available in the community (see Quality statement 6)n- details of referrals and follow-up appointments

claims.claim: The patient must receive a copy of the individualised care plan to take with them before being discharged, and a copy is also provided to their general practice and where appropriate their ongoing rehabilitation team or aged care provider before or at the time of discharge
claims.source_text: The patient must receive a copy of the individualised care plan to take with them before being discharged.

claims.claim: Quality statement 8 states that a patient who has had a stroke receives a follow-up assessment and review with appropriate multidisciplinary team input within six months of their stroke diagnosis, and that this is arranged before discharge
claims.source_text: A patient who has had a stroke receives a follow-up assessment and review, with appropriate multidisciplinary team input, within six months of their stroke diagnosis. This is arranged before discharge.

claims.claim: The follow-up appointment may be face-to-face or via telehealth and may not necessarily be the first or only follow-up with a healthcare provider
claims.source_text: It may be face-to-face or via telehealth, and may not necessarily be the first or only follow-up with a healthcare provider.

claims.claim: At the follow-up review clinicians should address medical and secondary prevention including medication adherence and indication, patient progress with lifestyle modifications and any pending investigation results; rehabilitation including re-assessing needs against goals and progress, recording functional status using a validated tool, and reviewing the choice of rehabilitation pathway; functional status including cognition, vision, fitness to drive, continence and equipment needs; psychosocial and vocational needs including re-assessing mood and if appropriate sexual dysfunction and reviewing or developing a return-to-work plan; and care coordination including reviewing the effectiveness of existing referrals
claims.source_text: Medical and secondary prevention: Review medication adherence and indication, patient progress with lifestyle modifications, and any pending investigation results.n- Rehabilitation: Re-assess rehabilitation needs against the patient's goals and progress. Record functional status at follow-up using a validated tool such as the Functional Independence Measure (FIM), modified Rankin Scale (mRS), Barthel Index, and Functional Autonomy Measurement System (SMAF). Review the choice of rehabilitation pathway to ensure rehabilitation continues to meet the patient's needs.n- Functional status: Assess cognition, vision, fitness to drive, continence and equipment needs.n- Psychosocial and vocational: Re-assess mood and, if appropriate, sexual dysfunction. Review or develop a return-to-work plan, which may include returning to voluntary work, community roles or ongoing carer responsibilities for partners, parents, children or grandchildren. Assess the person's engagement in community life and reintegration.n- Care coordination: Review the effectiveness of existing referrals and assess the need for further appointments with allied health, rehabilitation, or other community support services.

claims.claim: At the end of the follow-up appointment the patient, their GP and their ongoing rehabilitation team should be given an updated care plan
claims.source_text: Give the patient, their GP and their ongoing rehabilitation team an updated care plan at the end of the appointment (see Quality statement 7).

claims.claim: In 2023 there were an estimated 45,785 stroke events in Australia including 34,793 first-ever strokes, which equates to one stroke every 11 minutes
claims.source_text: In 2023, there were an estimated 45,785 stroke events in Australia, including 34,793 first-ever strokes, which equates to one stroke every 11 minutes.

claims.claim: The lifetime costs associated with strokes that occurred in 2023 exceeded $15 billion, which equates to almost $350,000 per person, and in 2022 stroke was the underlying cause of 8,400 deaths in Australia
claims.source_text: The lifetime costs associated with strokes that occurred in 2023 exceeded $15 billion, which equates to almost $350,000 per person. In 2022, stroke was the underlying cause of 8,400 deaths in Australia.

claims.claim: The Stroke Clinical Care Standard has been endorsed by 23 key organisations, and the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, the Queensland Aphasia Research Centre and Therapeutic Guidelines Ltd are listed as organisations that support the Standard
claims.source_text: The Stroke Clinical Care Standard has been endorsed by 23 key organisations … The following organisations support the Clinical Care Standard: - Royal Australian College of General Practitionersn- The Queensland Aphasia Research Centren- Therapeutic Guidelines Ltd.

claims.claim: The key Australian evidence source that underpins the Stroke Clinical Care Standard is the Stroke Foundation's Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
claims.source_text: The key Australian evidence source that underpins the Stroke Clinical Care Standard is the _Stroke Foundation's_ Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management.

claims.claim: Indicator 1a is the proportion of patients with a suspected stroke who were assessed by ambulance services using a validated stroke screening tool, and indicator 1b is the median time from first clinical contact to arrival at a hospital capable of providing appropriate time-critical stroke therapy
claims.source_text: Indicator 1a | Proportion of patients with a suspected stroke who were assessed by ambulance services using a validated stroke screening tool |n| Indicator 1b | Median time from first clinical contact to arrival at a hospital capable of providing appropriate time-critical stroke therapy for patients with a suspected stroke

claims.claim: Indicator 2a is the proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke who received intravenous thrombolytic therapy and indicator 2b is the median time from arrival at hospital to treatment with an intravenous thrombolytic agent
claims.source_text: Indicator 2a | Proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke who received intravenous thrombolytic therapy |n| Indicator 2b | Median time from arrival at hospital to treatment with an intravenous thrombolytic agent for patients with an ischaemic stroke

claims.claim: Indicator 2c is the proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke who received endovascular thrombectomy, indicator 2d the proportion transferred for endovascular thrombectomy, indicator 2e the median time from arrival at hospital to departure for patients transferred for endovascular thrombectomy, and indicator 2f the median time from arrival at hospital to endovascular thrombectomy for those who had it
claims.source_text: Indicator 2c | Proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke who received endovascular thrombectomy |n| Indicator 2d | Proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke who were transferred for endovascular thrombectomy |n| Indicator 2e | Median time from arrival at hospital to departure for patients with an ischaemic stroke transferred for endovascular thrombectomy |n| Indicator 2f | Median time from arrival at hospital to endovascular thrombectomy for patients with an ischaemic stroke who had endovascular thrombectomy

claims.claim: Indicator 2g is the median time from arrival at hospital to initiation of antihypertensive medicine for patients with an acute intracerebral haemorrhage and elevated systolic blood pressure on presentation, and indicator 2h is the median time from arrival at hospital to initiation of anticoagulation reversal for patients with an acute intracerebral haemorrhage taking an anticoagulant
claims.source_text: Indicator 2g | Median time from arrival at hospital to initiation of antihypertensive medicine for patients with an acute intracerebral haemorrhage and elevated systolic blood pressure on presentation |n| Indicator 2h | Median time from arrival at hospital to initiation of anticoagulation reversal for patients with an acute intracerebral haemorrhage taking an anticoagulant

claims.claim: Indicator 3a is the proportion of patients with a stroke who had documented treatment in a stroke unit, indicator 3b the median time from arrival at hospital to admission to a stroke unit, and indicator 3d the proportion who had a swallow screen or assessment completed before they were given any food, fluids or oral medication
claims.source_text: Indicator 3a | Proportion of patients with a stroke who had documented treatment in a stroke unit |n| Indicator 3b | Median time from arrival at hospital to admission to a stroke unit for patients with a stroke | … Indicator 3d | Proportion of patients with a stroke who had a swallow screen or assessment completed before they were given any food, fluids or oral medication

claims.claim: Indicators 4a, 4b and 4c are the proportions of patients with a stroke seen by a physiotherapist, a speech pathologist and an occupational therapist respectively within 48 hours of admission to hospital
claims.source_text: Indicator 4a | Proportion of patients with a stroke seen by a physiotherapist within 48 hours of admission to hospital |n| Indicator 4b | Proportion of patients with a stroke seen by a speech pathologist within 48 hours of admission to hospital |n| Indicator 4c | Proportion of patients with a stroke seen by an occupational therapist within 48 hours of admission to hospital

claims.claim: Indicator 4d is the proportion of patients with a stroke whose ongoing rehabilitation needs were assessed by a multidisciplinary team and documented before discharge to the community, and indicator 4e the proportion referred for ongoing rehabilitation before discharge from hospital
claims.source_text: Indicator 4d | Proportion of patients with a stroke whose ongoing rehabilitation needs were assessed by a multidisciplinary team and documented before discharge to the community |n| Indicator 4e | Proportion of patients with a stroke who were referred for ongoing rehabilitation before discharge from hospital

claims.claim: Indicator 5a is the proportion of patients with a stroke prescribed an antihypertensive medicine on discharge, indicator 5b the proportion with an ischaemic stroke prescribed a lipid-lowering medicine on discharge, and indicator 5c the proportion with an ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation prescribed an oral anticoagulant medicine on discharge
claims.source_text: Indicator 5a | Proportion of patients with a stroke prescribed an antihypertensive medicine on discharge from hospital |n| Indicator 5b | Proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke prescribed a lipid-lowering medicine on discharge from hospital |n| Indicator 5c | Proportion of patients with an ischaemic stroke and atrial fibrillation prescribed an oral anticoagulant medicine on discharge from hospital

claims.claim: Indicator 6a is the proportion of patients with a stroke where at least one family member or support person received information and practical assistance before discharge to the community, indicator 7a the proportion who had an individualised care plan on discharge, and indicator 8a the proportion who participated in a follow-up review within six months of diagnosis
claims.source_text: Indicator 6a | Proportion of patients with a stroke where at least one family member or support person received information and practical assistance to support the patient with their new daily needs before discharge to the community |n| Indicator 7a | Proportion of patients with a stroke who had an individualised care plan on discharge to the community |n| Indicator 8a | Proportion of patients with a stroke who participated in a follow-up review within six months of the diagnosis of their stroke

claims.claim: No benchmarks are set for the indicators by the Commission, and the definitions required to collect and calculate indicator data are specified online at the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's Metadata Online Registry METEOR
claims.source_text: No benchmarks are set for these indicators by the Commission. The definitions required to collect and calculate indicator data are specified online at the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's Metadata Online Registry ( METEOR).

claims.claim: The Standard applies to care provided in pre-hospital emergency settings primarily ambulance services, hospital settings including public and private hospitals, rehabilitation services and outpatient clinics, and some primary care settings
claims.source_text: This Clinical Care Standard applies to care provided in: - pre-hospital emergency settings, primarily ambulance servicesn- hospital settings, including public and private hospitals, rehabilitation services and outpatient clinicsn- some primary care settings.

claims.claim: The Standard relates to the care that adult patients should receive when they have or are suspected of having an ischaemic stroke or intracerebral haemorrhage, including patients who have a stroke while in hospital, and covers care from pre-hospital emergency service contact through hospital admission, discharge to the community and follow-up review within six months
claims.source_text: The Standard relates to the care that adult patients should receive when they have, or are suspected of having, an ischaemic stroke or intracerebral haemorrhage. This includes patients who have a stroke while in hospital. It covers the care provided from pre-hospital emergency service contact through hospital admission, discharge to the community and follow-up review within six months.
